query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, phase stability is governed by the magnitude of lattice distortion induced primarily by the atomic size mismatch of aluminum relative to the other elements. There is a critical aluminum concentration range over which the accumulated lattice strain energy offsets the ordering enthalpy that would otherwise trigger phase separation or precipitation, thereby stabilizing a single-phase solid solution that retains high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic single-phase Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with a low level of aluminum (e.g., below the critical threshold for ordering) exhibiting high configurational entropy and minimal lattice distortion.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the aluminum concentration in controlled batches of the alloy (while keeping Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni ratios nearly constant) and perform standardized thermal, mechanical, and environmental tests.
generation.conditions: Comparison under identical processing routes and test conditions: elevated temperatures (to assess high-temperature strength and phase stability), exposure to corrosive/radiation environments, and cryogenic mechanical testing to evaluate toughness.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion measured via shifts in lattice parameters (using X-ray diffraction) and the onset of ordered precipitate formation (observed by TEM/SEM), which mediates the balance between configurational entropy and ordering tendencies.
generation.mechanism: At moderate Al content, the enlarged atomic size of Al increases lattice strain energy enough to suppress ordering enthalpies that favor secondary phase formation. This mechanism stabilizes the single-phase state. Beyond a critical Al threshold, excessive strain promotes the nucleation of ordered precipitates (e.g., B2 or L12 phases), which alters the combination of mechanical and environmental properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Al content within the optimal range will remain as a disordered, single-phase solid solution with a balanced combination of high-temperature strength, corrosion/radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness. Alloys with Al concentrations exceeding the threshold will show detectable ordered precipitates along with corresponding changes in mechanical properties (e.g., increased yield strength yet potentially reduced toughness or environmental resistance).
generation.baseline: The baseline is the alloy with lower Al content (below the critical value) where the lattice distortion is insufficient to trigger significant ordering, leading to a relatively undistorted single-phase structure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in near-equiatomic Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni matrices with controlled Al variations. It applies within processing conditions where kinetic effects do not override thermodynamic stabilization (e.g., during equilibrium annealing) and may be limited when extrinsic factors (such as extreme cooling rates or non-equilibrium processing) affect the phase formation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical Al concentration range and the quantitative relationship between lattice distortion and phase stability are uncertain and likely depend on subtle processing conditions and compositional nuances. Moreover, the interplay between environmental resistance and the minor presence of ordered phases requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with systematically increased Al content spanning below and above the predicted critical threshold. Subject samples to identical homogenization and annealing treatments. Characterize the phase structure using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy, and measure mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, fracture toughness) at high, ambient, and cryogenic temperatures, as well as environmental resistance under accelerated corrosion/radiation exposure.
measurements: Lattice parameter shifts and evidence of ordered precipitates (via XRD/TEM)
Mechanical properties (tensile tests at varied temperatures)
Corrosion or radiation resistance performance metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if (a) no systematic correlation is found between aluminum content (and measured lattice distortion) and the emergence of ordered phases, or (b) if alloys with increased Al content do not exhibit the predicted changes in mechanical and environmental properties compared to the baseline single-phase alloy.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which were originally developed as concentrated solid solutions of multiple principal elements in equal, or near equal, atomic ratios, have drawn progressively increasing attention over the past decade. Unlike single principal-element alloys, their complex alloy compositions and elemental distribution, together with crystal lattice distortion induced by atomic-size mismatch (depending upon relative atomic sizes), can have a significant effect on the activity of their crystal defects and hence mechanical properties. Although HEAs were initially designed to benefit from single-phase stabilization,, single-phase HEAs are actually not that common, and of those that do exist, only a few display excellent damage-tolerance in the form of combinations of high strength, ductility, and toughness. The well-studied equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi Cantor alloy and its derivatives, in particular the CrCoNi alloy, show exceptional damage-tolerance which progressively improves at cryogenic temperatures, although even these alloys do not have yield (as opposed to ultimate tensile) strengths that are comparable to some advanced steels.
